extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent scholars, policymakers, USPTO officials
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains statutory standards and procedural rules in the America Invents Act (AIA) affecting post-issuance patent challenges (inter partes review, post-grant review, section 18 business-method review) including estoppel, burden of proof, discovery, sanctions, time limits, intervening rights, fees, venue, and prior-user rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 325(d) — Denial for previously presented same or substantially the same prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 325(d), second sentence, allows a request or petition to be rejected solely because the 'same or substantially the same prior art' previously had been presented to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scope is somewhat broader than pre-AIA §312(a)'s 'substantial new question' test because 325(d) permits rejection where the same or substantially the same prior art was earlier presented, whereas the earlier test could still require reexamination if the reference presented a 'substantial new question' even if considered previously for another purpose (see In re Swanson). Use of §325(d) is discretionary and the Director's decision to institute is 'final and nonappealable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel under §§315(e) and 325(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a petitioner completes a post-grant or inter partes review, that petitioner, as well as his real parties in interest and privies, will thereafter be estopped from raising in civil litigation, ITC proceedings, or any subsequent USPTO proceeding any issue that the petitioner actually raised and that was decided in the review, or any issue that the petitioner 'reasonably could have raised' in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The estoppel applies as soon as the PTAB enters a final written decision pursuant to §318(a) or §328(a) and is not delayed pending appeal. The AIA extended estoppel from only 'actually raised and decided' issues to issues that 'reasonably could have been raised,' a change from earlier law and prior proposals. The 'reasonably' modifier was intended to limit estoppel to prior art a skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have discovered. The provision applies to the petitioner and to 'real party in interest or privy,' raising practical privity considerations (e.g., potential effect on codefendants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to adjudicative proceeding and burden of proof (§§316(a)(4), 326(a)(4); §§316(e), 326(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall promulgate regulations establishing and governing inter partes and post-grant review as proceedings, and the petitioner shall have the burden of proving unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions effectively convert inter partes reexamination into an adjudicative proceeding in which the petitioner, rather than the Office, bears the burden of showing unpatentability. Section 316(a)(4) gives the Office discretion to prescribe regulations governing the new proceeding; section 316(e) assigns the petitioner the burden by preponderance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery limits in IPR and PGR (§§316(a)(5), 326(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in inter partes and post-grant review is limited and governed by an 'in the interest of justice' standard; additional discovery is restricted to particular limited situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery is more limited than in district-court litigation because the issues available in these proceedings are few and to limit burden, especially when instituted years after issuance. The standard restricts additional discovery to, e.g., minor discovery the PTO finds routinely useful or discovery justified by special circumstances. Given tight time deadlines, the PTO is anticipated to be conservative in granting discovery; limiting 'second-window' discovery reduces burden on patent owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for abuse (§§316(a)(6), 326(a)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO must promulgate regulations 'prescribing sanctions for abuse of discovery, abuse of process, or any other improper use of the proceeding, such as to harass or to cause unnecessary delay or an unnecessary increase in the cost of the proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may impose sanctions in the form of monetary fines (or payments to other parties) or restrictive orders relating to the proceedings, including dismissal of petitions or cancellation of claims. Regulations should address abusive tactics intended to harass, delay, or increase costs unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for completion of review (§§316(a)(11), 326(a)(11))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO is required to complete an inter partes or post-grant review within one year after institution, with a possible six-month extension for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deadline is intended to expedite proceedings (pre-AIA inter partes reexaminations often lasted 3–5 years). Reforms to meet deadlines include shifting from an examinational to adjudicative model, elevating the institution threshold (requiring petitioners to front-load their cases and tie challenges to particular validity arguments against particular claims) to prevent 'mushrooming' of challenges after institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening rights for new or amended claims (§§318(c), 328(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervening rights apply to new or amended claims incorporated into a patent in inter partes or post-grant review, affecting damages and the date from which they may accrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments that substantively alter claim scope can limit damages to the date of conclusion of review (section 252 first paragraph). Intervening-rights protection helps a challenger who, upon discovering patent-defeating prior art, narrows claims and wants to practice the invention without retrospective liability; the Federal Circuit has applied intervening rights to narrowing amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-user rights review and recommended changes (AIA §3(m))
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA required the USPTO Director to report to Congress findings and recommendations on prior-user rights in selected countries, with possible recommendations for U.S. law changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's recommendations included: (1) repealing the one-year requirement that commercial use be established a full year before the patent's effective filing date or public disclosure; (2) allowing a prior user to establish the defense by showing 'substantial preparations' for commercial use rather than requiring full commercial use; and (3) expanding the defense to apply to all subject matter (not just processes/products used in commercial processes). The Director noted the U.S. one-year limitation is more restrictive than other countries and may prevent use by U.S. manufacturers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for challenging USPTO decisions (AIA §9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amends statutes to make the Eastern District of Virginia, rather than the District of Columbia, the venue for challenges to various USPTO decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change corrects inconsistent statutory provisions that still authorized venue in D.C. even though the USPTO resides in the Eastern District of Virginia; the amendment makes venue consistent with the PTO's physical residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee-setting authority (AIA §10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 allows the USPTO to adjust all of its fees by regulation, subject to requirements and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees must be set to recover the aggregate cost of carrying out the USPTO's functions. The USPTO must provide advanced notice of proposed adjustments, seek comment from the Patent/Trademark Public Advisory Committees and the public, provide fee reductions to small and micro entities, and the fee-setting authority sunsets after seven years absent extension. The provision responded to PTO arguments that the agency needs flexibility to respond to workload challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification of current patent fee schedule (AIA §11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 codifies the patent fee schedule that was in effect at the time of the AIA's enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee Report noted this schedule represents a reference point for any future adjustments to the fee schedule by the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18 — Business-method patent review (scope and procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 creates an administrative proceeding to challenge 'covered business method patents' using standards and procedures of post-grant review, with several special rules limiting scope, standing, estoppel, prior art, stays, and temporal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: (1) limited to 'covered business method patents' and applies to patents before, on, or after enactment and throughout their life; (2) petitioners may file only if they (or their real parties in interest/privies) have been sued or charged with infringement of the patent; (3) estoppel after section 18 is limited to issues actually raised and decided in the section 18 review (though post-grant review's could-have-raised estoppel may apply to subsequent administrative proceedings); (4) prior art that can be raised is limited to publicly accessible art (pre-AIA §102(b) loss-of-right provisions cannot be asserted against a first-to-invent patent in this proceeding); (5) motions to stay a copending civil action are considered under a special four-factor test and are subject to interlocutory appeal of the district court's stay decision; (6) the proceeding became effective Sept. 16, 2012 and, absent extension, petitioning authority terminates Sept. 16, 2020. The section was explained as a relatively inexpensive alternative to litigation for challenging poor-quality business-method patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated institution threshold and front-loading requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA raised the threshold for instituting inter partes and post-grant review and required petitioners to front-load their case, tying challenges to specific validity arguments against particular claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elevated threshold was intended to prevent challenges from 'mushrooming' into additional arguments or claims after institution and to make proceedings more efficient and timely. This front-loading, combined with the elevated threshold, was a key reform to enable meeting one-year resolution deadlines and to reduce burdens on patent owners.
